items.title: Would You Go Back to a Time Before Smartphones If You Could?
items.description: Listen and subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Pocket Casts Back in the ’90s, before everyone had smartphones, were things just … better? Tech-focused nostalgia has become a potent cultural force in recent years, driving sales of “dumbphones,” iPods, CDs, and other retro technology. According to a 2023 survey , 67 percent of Americans wish they could go back to a time “before everyone was ‘plugged in.’” The psychologist behind that survey, Clay Routledge, has found that this sort of nostalgia is more than just a yearning to go backwards. “We can often feel overwhelmed in the moment and in the challenges we face today. It's hard to see past them. Nostalgia can help us step outside of that moment,” Routledge explains. Nostalgia can actually teach us how we want to live now, and in the future. The following is a transcript of the episode: [ Music ] Julie Beck: If you had one word—it can be a noun, it can be an adjective, it can be any part of speech that you want—to describe your overall relationship to technology at this moment in time. Voice memo: Antagonistic? Voice memo: Complicated. Voice memo: Fraught. Voice memo: Connection. Voice memo: I think of it as an addiction. Similar to how I relate to, like, sugar or anything else that I sort of compulsively overindulge in. Beck: What’s your word? Voice memo: Indentured. Voice memo: I was gonna say reluctant, but maybe that’s not right. Voice memo: Very frequent user. Beck: Okay, that’s a lot of words, but we’ll take it. Beck: I’m Julie Beck, a staff writer at The Atlanti c. Natalie Brennan: And I’m Natalie Brennan, a producer at The Atlantic . Beck: This is How to Touch Grass . Amy Poehler : Have you heard the young people say “touch grass”? Tiktok user : I switched to a dumb phone. This is the Nokia 2780. Amy Poehler : It’s like a term, basically, which is like, Get off your phones . Subway Takes : Smartphones are evil, they’re ruining society, and we need to just stop. 100% disagree. Amy Poehler : Get off the internet, and go outside and touch grass. Tiktok user 2 : I nominate everyone for the Touch Grass Challenge. Go outside and touch some grass like I’m doing right now. Go, go, go! [ Birds chirping ] Beck: In this season, we’ll be exploring the often-fraught, always-changing relationship people have with technology. And the ways that, in this moment, the terms of the relationship are being renegotiated. Brennan: Julie, the way that I would like to renegotiate my relationship to technology is that I would like to throw my phone in the East River. Beck: Natalie, you could throw your phone in the East River. Why don’t you? Brennan: It’s not really just about my phone. I wanna throw your phone in there too, Julie. But I can’t take everyone’s phone. Beck: Mmm. Brennan: So I think what I mean to say is that I yearn for a pre-phone era. Beck: I think we’re not the only ones who have this fantasy. It’s all over TikTok. TikTok user : What’s the biggest trend of 2026 gonna be? Analog. This past year, we’ve seen the rise of nostalgia; the switch from iPhone cameras to digital cameras… TikTok user 2 : Here’s how to actually be more analog in 2026. First, I wanna… TikTok user 3 : The analog era is here. And while audiences say they want to go offline, with Gen Z and millennials openly expressing their desires to break from an online world and find deeper… TikTok user 4 : I stopped using an iPhone three weeks ago and the effects have genuinely been profound. ​ Beck: In the past few years, there’s been no shortage of people advocating for reducing screen time. But another force that has been inspiring people to rethink how they use their devices lately is: nostalgia. [ Music ] Clay Routledge: We can often feel overwhelmed in the moment and in the challenges we face today. It’s hard to see past them. Nostalgia can help us step outside of that moment. Beck: Clay Routledge and his colleagues have been studying what’s behind this widespread yearning for a time before smartphones and before social media. Clay is a psychologist who specializes in nostalgia, and he’s also the author of Past Forward: How Nostalgia Can Help You Live a More Meaningful Life . Beck: Clay, hello, welcome! Routledge : Hi, Julie. Beck: I see you’ve got an Atari poster behind you. There’s some kind of video game that is too small for me to see what it is. What is it? Routledge: On the shelf, I’ve got an old Nintendo, the original NES. Then I’ve got the Robotron arcade game, which is an arcade from the ’80s, and the Atari poster. So yeah, lots of video-game nostalgia from different brands and decades. Beck: Oh, man. Perfect. Okay. It’s a nostalgia museum at your house. Routledge: It is indeed. Beck: Clay, just to get started, what is the point of being nostalgic about anything? Routledge: So nostalgia is, in psychological terms, what we call a self-regulatory resource. It helps us navigate life in important ways. We don’t know the future; it’s uncertain. And so it can also be a great source of anxiety. Nostalgia can help us step outside of that moment and say, You know, there’s a bigger picture. Right now, maybe I’m experiencing stress or loneliness, or I just went through some difficult challenge, but my life is full of other types of experiences, and if I had these more fulfilling experiences in the past, then I should be able to have them in the future. Beck: Yeah, I asked you about the past, and you immediately started talking about the future. Do people tend to misunderstand nostalgia by assuming, as I did, that it’s about the past? Routledge: So nostalgia, the dictionary definition is something like: a sentimental longing for the past . When you present it like that, then it makes sense that people would assume, well, nostalgia might even be people getting stuck in the past. Beck: Mm-hmm. Routledge: Or looking to the past too warmly and not, you know, dealing with their present realities head-on. Turns out that when people engage in this kind of nostalgic reflection, in a lot of ways they’re talking about their issues today, and they’re thinking about tomorrow. So nostalgia actually has this very forward-looking, unexpected, hopeful quality. We often are looking for specific things that can help us with particular challenges and anxieties we’re facing, so— Beck: Mmm. Routledge: —and I’m articulating this as if this is happening at some deliberate or conscious level, ’cause I’m talking about more of the scientific study of nostalgia and what we’ve learned from that kind of empirical work. But in reality, of course, this is just happening almost unconsciously. People are often using nostalgia without even realizing it. Beck: That makes sense to me when it comes to, you know, my own life and my own past experiences, right? But Clay, what about nostalgia for a time from before you were even alive? There was a stat from a survey you worked on that really struck me, which was you found that 60 percent of Gen Z wished that they could return to a time before everyone was, quote, “plugged in.” And the other generations said that too, but they actually lived through that time, whereas Gen Z has no actual memories of a time before the internet existed. So was that surprising to you? Routledge: It was. When we first found that, I was pretty surprised because most of the work, the research on nostalgia, including the research I’ve done, is focused on autobiographical— Beck: Mm. Routledge: —memory, but to your point, what we started to discover with that survey is: People actually have a longing for the past that predates them. Now, of course, if you’ve studied art and culture more abstractly, we’ve long known that people have favorite eras that they’re interested in, whether it’s the architecture or the music or the fashion. So we’ve known there’s this aesthetic nostalgia that’s historical— Beck: Mm-hmm. Routledge: —but what we were surprised to find is that young adults have so much to look forward to in the future, and we typically think of youth as very future-oriented, but the majority of them were saying that they longed for a time really before modern technology, but really before they were alive. And then since that survey, we’ve just done more and more surveys finding that around two-thirds of Gen Z adults say they’re nostalgic for a time before they were alive. Beck: Right. So this seems like a little bit more than just a like, We’re bringing low-rise jeans back , right?— Routledge: ( Laughs. ) Yeah. Beck: —if they’re saying they would like to live in the past. I mean, how common is it for generations to yearn that way for a past they never actually knew, or is something about this unique? Routledge: Yeah. There’s not a lot of research or really any research in previous generations when they were the same age as Gen Z. But we do know from our own work, in general, people tend to become nostalgic when they’re going through major life transitions or disruptions, or when the world feels particularly chaotic or uncertain. Beck: Mmm. Routledge: Regardless of whether you’re, you know, 20 or 60, sometimes there are sources of cultural inspiration that people wanna draw from in a more shared bank of memories that aren’t just your own, but are the memories we share as a culture. And here’s the key thing, I think, and this is the case with Gen Z too. It really isn’t the case that people want to live in the past. Beck: Okay. Routledge: If you start asking people Would they give up all of the modern advances? they say no. What they’re saying is they have a sentiment for some aspect of the past that they think that we’re missing today. I think there is something about Gen Z in this, you know, as digital natives who grew up in this era where this major transition from the analog world to the digital world, that seems to be sparking a particularly potent type— Beck: Yeah. Routledge: —of historical nostalgia. And then the irony is technology really is helping facilitate this. Because how are Gen Z adults learning about retro trends? They’re on TikTok, right? Beck: Yeah. Routledge: And so it’s funny how the technology that, on the one hand, is the source of frustration and anxiety is also the vehicle through which they’re being introduced to the analog world. Beck: Okay, so, I was wondering because, you know, when you say you wanna return to another era, an earlier era, maybe they’re not thinking about the things they would be dissatisfied with in the earlier era, right? Like— Routledge: Right. Beck: —lack of social progress that we have since made. It seems like you’re saying it tends to be about something particular that they are yearning for rather than, like, a holistic desire to go back to all the things. Routledge: Yeah, absolutely. You know, one of the things I think people don’t appreciate about nostalgia, ’cause it’s often portrayed as just repeating something. Beck: Mm. Routledge: And it really isn’t. It’s more of, like, a revising. There’s a creative process. Humans are really a progress-oriented species. We’re never content; we’re never satisfied. We’re always tinkering. We always think things can be a little bit better, and it’s frustrating, right? Because it often means we’re not ever just really happy. But that’s also the thing that drives us to positive change, and nostalgia’s very much an ingredient of that. [ Music ] Beck: So Natalie, I can remember really distinctly the last time that I was ever truly lost. Brennan: Mm-hmm. Beck: It was like two months before I would get my first smartphone. The year was 2013. Brennan: So you were—how old were you then? Beck: I was 23. Brennan: Okay. Beck: I was in St. Petersburg, Russia, and what I would do to get around in the days before I had Google Maps available on my phone all the time is I would look up directions on the computer before I left, and I would write them down, sometimes on my hand. Brennan: Totally. Beck: I had done this: I’d gotten my directions together, I had gone sightseeing, and I was heading back to my hotel. But I was so jet-lagged that I fell asleep on the bus, and when I woke up, I had no idea if I’d already missed my stop or not. Brennan: Oh no. Do you speak Russian? Beck: I definitely don’t. Um, but I went up to the bus driver anyways, to try to ask him if we had already passed the stop. A lot of people spoke English, you know, but he got really angry and was like, “You can’t talk to me while I’m driving.” So he wouldn’t talk to me, and I’m freaking out. And this young woman behind me, she can see how upset I am, and she speaks English. So she comes up and tells me, like, yes, we already passed the stop for my hotel. Lovely woman. She gets off the bus with me at the next stop— Brennan: No! Beck: —and she drew me a map on a piece of paper that she had, and she was like, “There’s this one really long road. You just have to walk on that road the whole way back.” And the hotel was on that road, so you would see it, you know, looming in the distance. And I remember she said, “It's really far. You’re gonna think that you’re never gonna get there, but I promise if you just keep walking on this one road, you will get back to the hotel.” Brennan: Oh my God. I’d be crying. Were you crying? Beck: Oh, for sure. Brennan: Yeah. ( Laughs. ) Beck: So anyway, I set off down the road for a really long time. It felt like miles, multiple miles. Brennan: You’re alone. Beck: I’m alone. I was traveling alone. When, out of nowhere, this man comes running towards me. Brennan: Nope. Beck: Well, it turns out he’s from a cruise ship that is docked nearby, and he is trying to find McDonald’s. Brennan: No. Beck: I tell him what happened. And he says, “Oh, well that’s the same direction as my cruise ship that I need to get back to. Like, I’ll just walk with you until you get back.” Eventually, my hotel appears on the horizon, finally. And there’s really no other word for it; he, like, scampers off into the night, and as he runs away, he shouts, “Goodbye, Julie. I love you.” Brennan: No! Beck: So anyway, I made it home safely. And that was the last time I was ever lost in my life. Brennan: Wow. I’m feeling both jealousy and awe, in that I will—I’ve never had that experience. I mean, I’ve been on public transportation, of course, while my phone has died. Beck: Yeah. Brennan: But I have never been an adult without a smartphone. Beck: I am kind of nostalgic for that memory, because it was one of those moments that really restores your faith in humanity. You know? Brennan: Yeah. Beck: Like, I was screwed, and people appeared, and they helped me when I really needed it. And that made me feel, like, swaddled tightly in the fabric of human community. And none of that would’ve happened if I had a smartphone, if I had Google Maps. Brennan: Yeah. I’ve only really ever had that experience manufactured for me. Beck: Really? Brennan: Yes. I went on this program in college. It was called the New England Literature Program. Beck: Okay. Brennan: And it’s basically living in cabins on a lake in New Hampshire for six weeks. And when you arrive, they take your phone for the remainder of the program. There’s no personal technology, no phones, no computers. Beck: Hmm. Brennan: You read Emerson, Thoreau. Beck: Of course you do. Who else would you read? Brennan: You visit Walden Pond. ( Laughs. ) And on the second day of the program is Get Lost Day. Beck: Okay. Brennan: In the morning, we learned how to use a compass, and then, promptly, were blindfolded, which now sounds like a cult, but it wasn’t— Beck: ( Laughs. ) Brennan: —to different locations, in groups, and then shown on a map where we were and where camp was, and told to get back by dinner. Beck: Wait, wait, wait. Where—like, describe to me the vibe of, like, where— Brennan: We were dropped off? Field. Beck: Field. End of sentence? Brennan: Yep. Beck: Field. Okay, okay, okay. Brennan: In the beginning, you’re quite confident that you’re on track, and I think a few hours in, it became quite clear to us that we weren’t making it back to camp, and that we would just find a ride later in the day. We would ask somebody to take us back to camp, and just kind of spent the day enjoying and exploring. Beck: Oh, wow. So you just pivoted. You were like, This is never happening. We’re not gonna find our way back. Brennan: No. Beck: Let's just be in this field. Brennan: We’re gonna—we are going to touch grass and vibe. Beck: Okay. Brennan: I’m sure we were walking for hours, but I think the bigger point, instead, was to, like, get to know each other. You’re placed into vulnerability. You’re going to share this experience. But I do think extremely fondly about the program. Those whole six weeks really just sparkle with nostalgia for me, and I really struggle to differentiate between how much of that experience was the “no tech” of it all— Beck: Hmm Brennan: —and how much of it was just the experience at large. [ Music ] Beck: Clay, what do you think the thing is that people who are nostalgic for the ’90s or the 2000s are wanting to bring forward and revise, as you say? Routledge: If I could sum it up using two words. Beck: That’d be great. Routledge: I would say control and community . Beck: Mm. Routledge: And the reason I’m picking those two words is because we’ve done, in addition to the surveys, we’ve done a number of qualitative projects that, you know, look at the types of nostalgic-related posts that Gen Z adults make on different social media and websites that they frequent. And what you often find is this sense that they love technology, but they wanna be in control of it, not feel controlled by it. Beck: Mm-hmm. Routledge: So it’s that more sense of intentional use, and this is why I think you see these interesting trends like Gen Z buying old iPods and, you know, they wanna have their new iPhone. Everybody wants to have the Uber app and all the different things that make our lives a little more convenient, but sometimes there’s a sense of like, Maybe there’s a more low-tech option that allows me just to listen to music . Beck: Yeah. Routledge: And the community. I think Gen Z’s figuring out that there’s something missing in computer-mediated social relationships. And on the one hand, the social media’s really useful ’cause it helps you organize events, meet people you would’ve never met. But at the same time, they look at this time period right before smartphones really became dominant, and they said, Oh, there’s a sense of freedom. There’s a sense of organic social life , and— Beck: You’re not looking at your phone the whole time. Routledge: —mm hmm. And they want to build that in. A lot of times, nostalgia’s framed in a very zero-sum sort of framework, where it’s like: You’re either for the past or you’re for the future. And I think what Gen Z’s showing us is they want both. And there’s something to say intergenerationally about this, which is maybe young people are learning about ’90s fashions on TikTok, but then what we often find is that sparks a conversation with older generations, whether it’s a parent or a coworker you know, or somebody in their run club, that they’re like, Oh, was life really like this? Did you really do this? And it creates a dialogue between generations, which I think, in this era of where everyone has their own screens and their own tailored content, is something that people feel like they’re really missing. Beck: Yeah. I remember my dad always used to talk about that—that sort of, like, shared experience of music, ’cause you had to, like, put on a record, and so everybody’s listening to the Rolling Stones whether they like it or not. And now, obviously, we just have our sort of, like, isolated pods, and you don’t know that I’m listening to that same Taylor Swift song like 10 times in a row, and you’ll never know. Routledge: ( Laughs. ) Now I know. Beck: Okay. Yeah, I did—yeah, now everybody knows. [ Music ] Beck: We’re gonna take a quick break. When we come back: Why is this analog nostalgia bubbling up now? Do you think it has anything to do with AI coming on the scene? [ Break ] Beck: Clay, why do you think nostalgia for analog technology is so popular right now ? Does the buzz about AI have anything to do with it? Routledge: I think AI is part of it, because if machines can do all this cognitive work, and maybe even creative work, that we thought was the distinct domain of humanity, now you’re seeing more of this holistic thinking of like, what is the essence of being a person? Beck: Mm-hmm. Routledge: And this nostalgia, I think, is really helping people get that sense of embodiment, of like, this isn’t just cognition. There’s something about emotion, spirituality, living in the world, having these tactile sensory experiences, in-person, real contact with other real human beings. Beck: Just with like, all the parts of life that are more than just being a brain in a jar, basically? Routledge: Yeah, that’s a great way of putting it. And if you look at a lot of the consumer nostalgic trends, many of them driven by Gen Z, they’re very much that, right? They’re the rise of independent bookstores , the growth of music festivals , book clubs , game nights, old tech, technology that’s not online that you have to—I was talking to somebody the other day about retro video games, and they were saying, “Well, one thing that’s really cool is you have to sit next to each other to play, like two players.” Beck: Yeah. Routledge: You’re not playing online. And so I think there’s this idea that even if it’s technology, even if it’s like video games or music, you mentioned vinyl records, which, you know, one of the big drivers of vinyl-record sales is Gen Z. They’re these low-tech, retro-tech trends that really seem to be about being out in the world, handling things, engaging with people. That’s a big driver of this. [ Music ] Beck: Natalie, let’s play a little game where I name a thing that people might be nostalgic for, and then try to psychoanalyze what it means about what they actually want from their relationship to technology. Brennan: Okay. Beck: Okay, my first one: I see a lot of memes about people missing the days when people had computer rooms in their home. Like, picture a big wooden entertainment center with a big monitor. The shelves are all covered in CD-ROMs, and then the meme says something like, We used to respect the computer. What does this mean? Brennan: This is really giving that control element that Clay was talking about— Beck: Mm. Brennan: —in that we still want to honor our computer. We love computer time, right? But I think we miss that separation in which your technology wasn’t on you at all times, right? My phone is kind of just a mini computer at this point. Beck: Yeah. Brennan: So I think we like having some separation of, like, now it’s time for me to go in the computer room, and when I’m done, it’s done. Does that resonate with you? Beck: Yeah. It’s a deliberate choice to go in the computer room and sit your butt in front of it and use it and then leave. Brennan: And then leave. Beck: I think you’re onto something. Okay, I am personally very nostalgic for Google Reader— Brennan: Mm. Beck: —which, for those who may not know, it was an aggregation service for websites’ RSS feeds, which doesn't sound fun, but it was. Brennan: ( Laughs .) Beck: Um, basically, in the late 2000s, I would use this to, like, follow all my favorite blogs and cooking websites and news sources, and it was all in one place. What do you think I’m actually longing for here? Brennan: Okay, well, I think for me what comes up here is feeling like the internet isn’t anymore curated towards what I wanna see. So for example, like I’ll open my Instagram app and I no longer see posts by my friends and family who I follow, but instead I see a lot of pushed posts. The algorithm just sends me what it thinks I wanna see. And so maybe you’re yearning for that time where the internet was curated to your niche hobbies and what you are actually interested in. Beck: As opposed to just a bunch of slop. Brennan: Okay, I wanna ask you one. I am also one of the analog Gen Zers who love to shoot film and collect old cameras. Thoughts? Beck: Um, I don’t know about you, but sometimes I pick up my phone to take a picture of probably my cats, and before I know it, I’m, like, sucked into a million other things on my phone. Brennan: Mm-hmm. Beck: So I think, maybe, there’s also something about, like, when you wanna take a picture, you just wanna take a picture, and taking that function out of the everything device and letting it just be its own thing, maybe. Brennan: It’s that. Beck: Crushed it. [ Music ] Beck: Clay, I was fascinated to learn that back in the 17th to 19th century, nostalgia was considered a disease , and doctors tried to cure it with leeches. I read that there was this one American doctor who kind of thought the way to cure it was just bullying people, like shaming them with public ridicule. And, obviously, we no longer think nostalgia is literally a disease, but I think a thread of that negative attitude remains. I feel like I sometimes hear other people talk about nostalgia as though you’re trying to hide from reality, and maybe, you know, you should be a little embarrassed. Do you see that reaction from people when it comes to this current cultural yearning for a pre-digital era that, okay, it’s not a disease , but maybe it’s still not good for you? Routledge: Yeah, definitely. People seem to have this view of nostalgia as anti-progress or holding people back from progress, and I spend a fair amount of time trying to disabuse them of that view and show them decades of empirical research. It really isn’t holding people back. We all have to adjust to change, and nostalgia helps people navigate that in the best way that they can. Even people who don’t think nostalgia’s a barrier to progress, oftentimes you see it characterized as a waste of time. Beck: Hmm. Routledge: Like, it’s a trivial thing, and it’s a distraction at best. Actually, nostalgia increases goal motivation . It increases a sense of meaning in life. It increases optimism. It makes people more creative . It increases empathy . Most nostalgic memories are social memories, so nostalgia actually pushes us towards each other. Beck: When you’re saying that some people are seeing nostalgia as an impediment to progress, do you think some of that has to do with the sort of Make America Great Again brand of nostalgia where, like you’re saying, people are looking to the past to potentially bring things into the future, but sometimes what they want to bring into the future is, for instance, stricter and more stereotypical gender roles? Routledge: So declinism is the view that things are getting worse and the past was better, whereas nostalgia really is just more of this warm feeling for the past, and I think the two are often conflated. We also find, overwhelmingly, that most of the time, nostalgia in general makes us see the humanity in other people. Or another way of saying it is: Nostalgia might be helping people wrestle with declinism— Beck: I see. Routledge: —and hopefully in a more productive and constructive way. A lot of Gen Z might feel like, oh, things are going in the wrong direction and their future’s gonna be worse than the future of previous generations. And there's certainly, you know, a lot of data that support that. Nostalgia’s helping them feel agentic and say, Well, you know what? We can change that. We can do something else . Beck: It just feels surprising when you see an era that was not a great time for a lot of people recast as something to be nostalgic for. Routledge: There are people that have nostalgia for COVID, which, again, not that long ago. Beck: Not that fun, famously. Routledge: Not that fun. But you know what? What’s interesting is, that wasn’t that surprising to me. When I first started doing this research, I was a professor at the University of Southampton in England. And Southampton’s a city that was heavily bombed during World War II, as a port city, and a good chunk of the city was destroyed. Not a good time. When we were doing this research, this was a little over 20 years ago, we were collecting nostalgic narratives from older British adults. Many of them were young children during that time, and they had this nostalgia. Beck: Yeah. Routledge: But what it was is they were saying, Well, this was a time that was defining, character defining. It wasn’t a pleasant time. It shaped our character, shaped our view of the world, shaped our ability to appreciate what’s important in life. Beck: So how does this sort of personal, individual nostalgia, right, then grow and end up becoming a cultural moment or an internet trend? Routledge: ’Cause a lot of times what people are really looking for with nostalgia is an opportunity to share memories. Beck: Hmm. Routledge: Oftentimes, nostalgia is portrayed as this very isolating, personal experience. After all, this is in your head. You’re experiencing this emotion. But people love opportunities where they can talk about nostalgic experiences, particularly ones where they might have their own idiosyncratic memory of it, but it was shared with other people. Beck: Mmm. Routledge: I think this is why people have a nostalgia for television where you had to wait and everyone had to watch the show at the same time, and then the next day we could all talk about it. Beck: Yeah. Routledge: You know, people are looking for ways to make contact over shared experiences where their personal nostalgia is woven into a broader cultural nostalgia that connects us. Beck: And we’ve talked about control a good amount, and, you know, obviously we can’t actually travel back in time to an era when nobody had smartphones. Sam Altman is gonna keep making new iterations of ChatGPT, and I have no control to stop him. But do the things that we’re nostalgic for hold any lessons for how we can exert the control that we do have over the role tech plays in our lives? Routledge: When the broader world outside of yourself, when you scale out, when it feels like you don’t have any control over that, that can be anxiety provoking; if you just focus your attention on your corner of the world, we actually do have a lot more control. Agency often happens at a local and at a personal level. You can help your neighbors. You can help your family. You can help your friends. You can be involved with those things. And even media engagement’s a way to remind ourselves of that. It’s like, Yeah, I don’t have control over the next internet iteration of a particular technology, but I can go to that retro store down the street and buy some Blu-ray discs and have a movie night at my house and have some people over. Beck: Yeah. Routledge: So I think people are really seeking that kind of experience. Beck: Are you seeing people actually acting on this pre-digital nostalgia? Routledge: There is an increased sales in physical media. The live-music market is growing. Mass attendance is up, like young people going to church. Beck: Right. Routledge: The number of independent bookstores and the number of chain bookstores, like Barnes & Nobles, is growing. There does seem to be something changing in our culture that’s a push back to the in-person and the analog. Beck: Clay, I’ve noticed at many times in this conversation that you’re very optimistic about Gen Z, which is not how I often hear people talking about that generation, especially when it comes to tech. So I’m curious to hear a little bit more about how you’re thinking about it and whether Gen Z is kind of leading this trend for other generations. Routledge: My thinking on Gen Z has really evolved, so I’m way more bullish on Gen Z— Beck: Hmm. Routledge: —than I used to be. So I’m a psychologist, and so when all of this research was coming out about these growing mental-health problems that young people were facing and how Gen Z reported higher rates of depression, anxiety, loneliness, pessimism for the future, like everyone else, I was like, This isn’t good. Young people are supposed to be the ones that are optimistic. They’re supposed to be the ones that look to the future with possibility, and that didn’t seem to be the case. But then I started really studying this historical nostalgia and started seeing, like, yeah, Gen Z has their challenges, and maybe mental health is one of them, but they’re not just sitting there doing nothing about it. They’re using their creativity and their problem-solving capacities that all humans have to do something about it, and I feel like this historical nostalgia that they’re engaging in is just one example of that. It’s not people my age that remember that time. It’s Gen Z that are saying, Hey, maybe we’re spending too much time online . And so, for instance, there’s surveys showing that Gen Z are the generation most likely to report disconnecting from their digital devices. Beck: Hmm. Routledge: So now I have a different view. It’s a, you know, it’s not a certain view, of course. It’s an optimistic view, though, that Gen Z might not only be doing better than we think they are in navigating their challenges and having the agency to do so, but they actually might lead us out of this mess. They might be the ones that remind the rest of us that there is an in-person, real-world life. So, you know, I often say that it’s common for people to feel sorry for Gen Z and worry that as digital natives, they were born too late to really appreciate the analog world. Beck: Hmm. Routledge: But in reality, it might be that they’re the generation that leads us back to it. [ Music ] Brennan: Mmmm …? Beck: It sounds like you’re not so sure, Natalie. Brennan: I said I wanted to throw my phone in the East River, and suddenly now I am tasked with healing everyone’s relationship to technology. Beck: Not just you. Just you and your entire generation are responsible for the rest of us? Uh … Brennan: I don’t know. I get so frustrated about this because I feel like I hear it all the time. It’s the same thing with climate change. Like, We’ll be the ones that need to fix all of it. I’m just like, This list is getting a little bit long. We’ve got a lot to fix now. Beck: Honestly, I think what talking to Clay made me realize is that so many of us are just looking for inspiration on how to move forward with technology in a way that doesn’t feel bad. Because we have to live in 2026. Brennan: Yeah. Beck: It’s never gonna be 1996 again. Brennan: Right. I think as a joint mission, then I can get behind that. Beck: When, like, Gen Z doesn’t have to be the leader, nobody’s the leader, nobody’s the follower, we’re just figuring it out together. Brennan: Yeah, or even bigger picture, when I feel like this is just on each one of us individually versus, you know, something that we’re all just, like, trying to renegotiate together. When it’s an individual mission, I think that’s maybe when I go escapist mode, when I go, like, fantasize about throwing the phone in the river, I wanna go back in time, back to those New England woods, to no phone. Beck: Back to your fields, back to your compass. Brennan: Yeah, back to my grass. [ Music ] Beck: That’s all for this episode of How to Touch Grass . This episode was hosted by me, Julie Beck, and co-hosted and produced by Natalie Brennan. Our editors are Claudine Ebeid and Jocelyn Frank. Fact-check by Gisela Salim-Peyer. Our engineer is Rob Smierciak. Rob also composed some of the music for this show. The executive producer of audio is Claudine Ebeid, and the managing editor of audio is Andrea Valdez. Beck: Next time on How To Touch Grass: Ashleigh Golden: A priest, a partner, a therapist, or a friend—these people have natural limits. They get tired. They push back. But the chatbot doesn't. Elias Aboujaoude: These programs are trained to be endlessly validating and endlessly agreeable. Beck: Turning to AI for help with anxiety could actually end up making you more anxious. That’s next time on How to Touch Grass .

items.title: Sandbondtenga/Tourisme: des membres de l’AJK en immersion pour promouvoir le patrimoine culturel
items.description: Sandbondtenga/Tourisme: des membres de l'AJK en immersion pour promouvoir le patrimoine culturel Kaya, 23 juil. 2026 (AIB) – L'Association des Journalistes des Koulsé (AJK), avec l'appui du ministère de la Communication, de la Culture, des Arts et du Tourisme, a organisé jeudi à Kaya une journée d'immersion sur des sites touristiques et culturels de la province du Sandbondtenga afin d'inciter les professionnels des médias à promouvoir davantage le tourisme interne. L'activité, inscrite dans la dynamique nationale de valorisation du patrimoine culturel, a débuté par une communication sur la cartographie des sites touristiques des Koulsé, animée par Vincent Ouédraogo, agent de la Direction régionale de la Communication, de la Culture, des Arts et du Tourisme (DRCAT). Selon le coordonnateur de l'AJK, Emil Segda, la région dispose de plus de 160 sites touristiques et culturels, dont 64 classés, mais ces richesses restent encore peu connues. « Beaucoup de journalistes ignorent ces potentialités. Cette immersion leur permettra de mieux les connaître afin de réorienter leurs productions vers la promotion du patrimoine culturel et touristique », a-t-il déclaré, saluant l'accompagnement du ministère de la communication, de la culture, des arts et tourisme. Les participants ont ensuite visité les hauts fourneaux de l'Association culturelle Passaté, témoins de l'ancienne métallurgie du fer, puis le musée communal de Kaya. Le guide des hauts fourneaux, Roger Bamogo, a estimé que cette initiative contribuera à accroître la visibilité du site et a plaidé pour sa réhabilitation afin de préserver ce patrimoine au bénéfice des générations futures. Au musée communal, Vincent Ouédraogo a invité les journalistes à relayer davantage les atouts touristiques de la région afin d'encourager les populations à visiter ces sites. Présente à l'activité, la directrice régionale de la Communication, de la Culture, des Arts et du Tourisme des Koulsé, Safiata Oubda, a salué cette initiative de l'AJK, qu'elle a qualifiée d'importante contribution à la promotion du tourisme interne. Agence d'information du Burkina AIO/bak

items.title: Youcef Belaïli au MC Alger : son salaire suscite la controverse
items.description: Youcef Belaili , est de retour en championnat Algérie, après deux saisons passées en Tunisie, avec l’ES Tunis. L’attaquant international algérien s'est engagé avec le MC Alger après plusieurs semaines de négociations et de rebondissements. Pour ce retour au Doyen où il a joué durant la saison 2023-2024, l’ancien joueur d’Ajaccio percevra avec un salaire mirobolant de 65.000 euros par mois soit près de 18 millions de dinars (1,8 milliards de centimes au taux de change parallèle), selon plusieurs médias spécialisés dont Compétition. Dans ce contexte, une interrogation demeure : comment le champion d’Algérie en titre compte-t-il rémunérer sa nouvelle recrue, alors que la FAF a plafonné les salaires des joueurs professionnels ? Le feuilleton du transfert de Belaïli de l’ES Tunis au MC Alger a pris fin le 24 juillet. Dans un communiqué publié le jour même, le club tunisien a annoncé avoir clos définitivement le dossier du renouvellement du contrat de son joueur. L’ES Tunis a expliqué qu'après « l'épuisement de toutes les phases de négociation et l'expiration de tous les délais convenus entre les différentes parties », il a été décidé de mettre un terme aux discussions avec son désormais ex-attaquant. L'Espérance a rappelé qu'un accord de principe avait été conclu le 5 juin entre les dirigeants du club et Youcef Belaïli. Celui-ci prévoyait une prolongation de deux saisons afin de préserver « les piliers de l'équipe et d'assurer sa stabilité sportive ». Le club affirme également avoir accompagné l'international algérien dans son litige avec la FIFA, notamment en mettant à sa disposition tous les documents nécessaires pour défendre son dossier devant le Tribunal arbitral du sport (TAS). En mars dernier, la FIFA a infligé une suspension d’une année à Belaili, dans le cadre du litige qui l’oppose à son ancien club, AC Ajaccio où il a évolué durant la saison 2022-2023 Après deux rendez-vous manqués pour effectuer la visite médicale et signer le contrat, l'ES Tunis a finalement décidé de mettre un terme aux négociations. « Tout en souhaitant à Mohamed Youcef Belaïli pleine réussite pour la suite de sa carrière, la direction assure que l'intérêt de l'Espérance Sportive de Tunis, le prestige du club, le respect de sa parole et de ses engagements demeurent toujours prioritaires », conclut le communiqué. Le MC Alger officialise un accord avec Youcef Belaili Quelques heures plus tard, peu avant minuit, le MC Alger a annoncé avoir trouvé un accord définitif avec Youcef Belaïli. Le club précise que le joueur retrouvera les Vert et Rouge pour la saison 2026-2027 et que « les deux parties se sont entendues sur l'ensemble des modalités financières ainsi que sur les différents autres aspects du contrat ». Toutefois, le Mouloudia précise que cet accord ne prendra officiellement effet qu'après la décision définitive du Tribunal arbitral du sport (TAS) concernant la sanction infligée au joueur par la FIFA et après une visite médicale concluante. Belaïli relance le débat sur le plafonnement des salaires des joueurs par la FAF Selon Compétition, Youcef Belaïli a négocié un salaire de 65.000 euros par mois pour un contrat de deux saisons avec le MC Alger. Cette information soulève toutefois des interrogations au regard des nouvelles règles instaurées par la Fédération algérienne de football (FAF). Depuis la saison 2025-2026, la FAF a adopté un nouveau contrat-type pour les joueurs professionnels. Celui-ci prévoit un salaire mensuel plafonné à 300 000 dinars, soit environ 2 000 euros au taux de change officiel. Les nouvelles dispositions prévoient également que les salaires et les primes de l'ensemble des joueurs, qu'ils soient algériens ou étrangers, soient versés en dinars algériens. En pratique, ce plafond concerne toutefois le salaire fixe. Les contrats peuvent également inclure une prime à la signature ainsi que des primes de performance, qui représentent une part importante de la rémunération globale. À ce stade, ni le MC Alger ni Youcef Belaïli n'ont communiqué les détails financiers du contrat. Les informations avancées par la presse spécialisée n'ont pas été confirmées officiellement. Si le montant de 65 000 euros mensuels venait à être confirmé, il relancerait le débat sur l'application des nouvelles règles salariales mises en place par la FAF et sur les mécanismes permettant aux clubs de rémunérer leurs joueurs vedettes. L’article Youcef Belaïli au MC Alger : son salaire suscite la controverse est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: The Newcomer
items.description: Read more about the Democrats who might run for president in 2028 here . G overnor Wes Moore doesn’t care about saving the Democratic Party; if anything, he thinks it has stood in his way. When we met up in May, he quoted Jay-Z: “ Industry shady, it need to be taken over .” The 2001 track is about Jay-Z’s rise to fame, and the ways the recording industry tried to exploit and co-opt him because he was “raisin’ the status quo up .” Moore was talking about a failed political system, and a Democratic Party that, he told me, “tried as hard as they could to get me not to run.” Jay-Z describes himself as a “renegade,” and Moore would like to be seen in a similar light—as the outsider who got himself to the top. Moore is the first Black governor of Maryland and the only Black governor serving in America today. At 47, he’s a relative newcomer to politics—he was the head of Robin Hood, a poverty-fighting foundation, until 2021—but he’s already being discussed as a possible presidential candidate in 2028. He’s just the kind of Bronze Star–winning, God-praising, son-of-an-immigrant Rhodes Scholar whom many Democratic voters would see as a dream candidate (although he denied to me that he was considering running). But so far, his tenure as governor has been far from smooth. In May 2025, he surprised many people by vetoing a bill establishing a commission to study the economic effects of slavery and racism on the state’s citizens and to recommend policies that could include reparations. Black legislators were outraged, and the Maryland General Assembly eventually overrode his veto. Moore defended his decision by dismissing the commission as a body conducting mere academic research, when what people needed was real change: “I am not a believer in studies, commissions,” he told me. “I’m like, Are we doing the work or not? ” He pointed to big investments in HBCUs and a mass pardon for cannabis convictions as proof of his progressive accomplishments. [ Richard D. Kahlenberg: The Democrats can’t let go of racial preferences ] Moore likes to portray himself as an independent actor, beholden to no one. He has signed legislation that prevents 16- and 17-year-olds from being tried as adults for some crimes, and also increased funding for the police. He has, he boasted to me, vetoed “more bills than any Democratic governor in the history of the state of Maryland” because he doesn’t believe in passing “unfunded mandates.” And he doesn’t care whether the party likes it or not: “I didn’t win because of the Democratic Party,” he said. “I won in spite of the Democratic Party.” He added: “I don’t come from nothing, and I didn’t need nothing, and I’m not owned by anybody. When I’m making my decisions, there is no party boss that I call.” Although this message seems tailor-made for this moment, in which so many Americans are simultaneously highly partisan yet disgusted by both parties, Moore’s approval rating in Maryland has fallen below 50 percent for the first time. (He’s still expected to win easily in the November election—he won 88 percent of the vote in the June primary, and one of his staffers shared with me an internal poll that found a higher approval rating.) He’s facing a number of challenges, particularly the dogged perception that he lacks authenticity—that he hasn’t been honest about who he really is. Moore has a politician’s powder-white smile and a bald head that shines like glass. I met him this spring, in Selma, Alabama, where he’d gone to commemorate the anniversary of Bloody Sunday, when about 600 civil-rights marchers were attacked on the Edmund Pettus Bridge. He began the weekend with a speech at Brown Chapel AME Church. “I know we are built for this, because I know what we are built of,” he told the mostly Black crowd. He listed heroes of the civil-rights movement and then said, “This is our time,” holding up his index finger like a Baptist preacher. Everywhere he went, lines formed. And he played his role perfectly. A bear hug for Governor J. B. Pritzker of Illinois. A selfie for a Black teenager with braces. “Good morning! Good morning! Good morning! How’s everybody doin’?” Then, pulling on the words like a southerner: “Alllll riiiiiight.” An hour or so later, at the Historic Tabernacle Baptist Church, his words tipped toward preaching: “I know where my worthiness comes from, and it does not come from Washington, D.C.” A few weeks later, on the Baltimore Orioles’ Opening Day, he stepped out of a black SUV wearing an orange jersey with his name on the back, and a man rushed up to him: “Sign my baseball for when you run for president.” “Not going to happen,” Moore quickly responded—while signing his name. Over the next few months, I watched Moore go from boat ride to baseball game to matcha tasting to college-graduation speech. In every situation, he knew exactly who to be. By the time he quoted Jay-Z to me, I understood that he had me pegged, too. Don Smallwood for The Atlantic Moore and his wife, Dawn, speaking to families at their official residence in June. I was fascinated by Moore’s ability to adapt to his different audiences. I grew up having to do the same, and although I appreciate that I can connect with people from both elite and underprivileged backgrounds, I wish I were as much of a natural as he is. Even as a journalist at The Atlantic , I still find myself sometimes intimidated, my voice trembling. Moore moved like water. But this may be one reason some voters struggle to trust him. When I asked people I know in Maryland, many of them Black, what they think of the governor, I heard things such as He doesn’t say what he means and We don’t know what his agenda is . They thought it was weird that he won without having any political experience. That distrust has been fueled by persistent negative reporting from conservative media outlets. At the Orioles game, a white man in a USA shirt said, “I appreciate you, Gov,” as Moore autographed his collection of baseball cards. Then Moore walked onto the field, and many people in the stadium booed. He smiled and clapped for himself, and seemed to take no notice of the crowd’s displeasure. About that Bronze Star. Moore has been accused of making what The Washington Free Beacon called “a litany of false statements about his family history, his upbringing, and his academic, athletic, and military achievements.” The accusations range from minor to significant, and begin with his hometown. The text on the back cover of his 2010 book, The Other Wes Moore: One Name, Two Fates , reads: “Two kids named Wes Moore were born blocks apart.” Both “grew up fatherless in similar Baltimore neighborhoods and had difficult childhoods.” In fact, Moore’s first years were spent in Takoma Park, Maryland—a nice suburb of Washington, which I know because I live about five minutes away. The book itself does mention that his family home was on “the border of Maryland and Washington, D.C.” But many people who read the book still come away with the impression that Moore was born and raised in Baltimore. It’s true that he grew up fatherless. Moore was 3 when his father died of a virus; he believes that a racist health-care system gave him shoddy treatment. His mother moved with Moore and his sisters to the Bronx, to be closer to her family. He attended the elite Riverdale Country School, but after his grades dropped and he got caught with a smoke bomb in the locker room as a prank, his mother sent him to Valley Forge Military Academy, in Pennsylvania. (His grandparents took out a second mortgage to help pay the tuition.) He moved back to Baltimore only as a college student, to go to Johns Hopkins University. He was living there in 2015 when the city erupted in protests following the death of Freddie Gray, who suffered a spinal-cord injury while inside a police van. Moore co-authored an account of that period with Erica L. Green, Five Days: The Fiery Reckoning of an American City . (“I am from Baltimore,” he wrote in that book.) He later kept a home in the city while commuting to Robin Hood in New York. After his Baltimore bona fides came under scrutiny in 2022, his campaign said that he had asked his publisher to correct the promotional text on The Other Wes Moore , and it did for later editions. Moore quickly learned to be more careful: “I’m not a Baltimorean by birth, but I’m a Baltimorean by choice,” he told a crowd in 2022. But a pattern had been established—or at least a line of attack. In 2010, Stephen Colbert described Moore, a guest on The Colbert Report , as a recipient of a Bronze Star for his service in Afghanistan, where he’d served in 2005 and 2006. The trouble was that he didn’t have a Bronze Star. When reporters raised questions about the medal, Moore’s staff insisted that he’d never told anyone that he had won it, and so he wasn’t responsible for the error. But in 2024, The New York Times obtained Moore’s application for a White House fellowship in 2006 in which he’d written, “the 82nd Airborne Division have awarded me the Bronze Star Medal.” He had an explanation for that too: The senior officer who had helped Moore write the application told him that he was going to get the medal, and so he should include it; the fact that it never actually arrived was embarrassing, but not unusual in the chaos of wartime. And after the controversy surfaced, the military did indeed award him a Bronze Star —just 18 years late. [ From the July 2026 issue: Being Black in Pete Hegseth’s military ] Then the Free Beacon ran a story questioning Moore’s account that his great-grandfather had moved to Jamaica because he’d been targeted by the KKK, based on the fact that reporters couldn’t find contemporaneous newspaper or archival accounts to verify it. This charge seemed more than a little forced—as did the many stories about Moore’s thesis at the University of Oxford. In that same White House fellowship application, he wrote that he’d received his degree in 2003 or 2004, but it wasn’t formally recorded until 2005. He also listed the title of his thesis as “The Rise and Ramifications of Radical Islam in the Western Hemisphere,” but it was later titled “Radical Islam in Latin America in the Late 20th Century and Its Middle Eastern Roots.” Also, the thesis is not stored in Oxford’s Bodleian Library—though there is no requirement for theses to be kept there, and many aren’t. Moore told The Baltimore Sun that he wasn’t “going to spend a second of my time trying to dig” a copy up. Marvin Joseph / The Washington Post / Getty Moore officially receives the Bronze Star Medal in 2024. If you’re a little bored, you’re right to be. Some people have compared Moore to Barack Obama, and the demands for him to release more records to back up his past inevitably reminded me of the “birther” conspiracy. At least that conspiracy had some stakes. How much should anyone care that in 2006, Moore said he’d been named to the Maryland College Football Hall of Fame when in fact he had been honored only by a College Football Hall of Fame affiliate called the National Football Foundation? Moore expresses regret for not being clear about the Bronze Star, but when I asked him about the attacks on his truthfulness in general, he dismissed them. “Do you know who has never attacked my military record? The United States Army,” he said. He told me he lived by a code: “You do not lie, cheat, or steal.” In fact, he said, he was being accused of dishonesty precisely because he was so honest. “It’s basic laws of warfare: You go after your opponent’s strength.” And he pointed out that these accusations surfaced only after he started gaining support. “I went a whole year on a campaign, and no one had a word to say about me,” he said. “And then out of nowhere, it was like the deluge began,” and people from “the right wing started putting stuff out.” The Baltimore Sun , which has devoted much space to these controversies, has indeed moved rightward under a new owner, the television magnate David Smith, and the conservative Free Beacon ’s tagline is a promise to cover “the enemies of freedom in the way the mainstream media won’t.” Moore told me that Obama had given him advice on surviving these kinds of attacks as a politician, saying, “Listen, this is the part of the game that everyone hates.” But if the questions about Moore’s honesty have been amplified by his opponents, they still trace back to an uncomfortable set of facts: Moore allowed people to call him a Bronze Star–winning Baltimore kid, when the story was more complicated. In April, one of Moore’s biggest legislative priorities—a redistricting plan that could have helped Democrats pick up a seat in the midterms—died when William Ferguson, the Democratic president of the state Senate, refused to bring it up for a vote. It was “ too risky ,” Ferguson argued: The new map could be challenged, and a ruling could leave their party worse off. Ferguson is now pushing to get a constitutional amendment before Maryland voters in November that would better shore up any new map from legal challenges. Moore has framed the legislature’s caution as timidity, but Ferguson has a different take. He told me that Moore had created confusion by waiting months before coming out in favor of the plan, and suggested that the governor embraced it only after Gavin Newsom gained national attention for pushing through a new map in California. “I don’t think that timing was a coincidence,” Ferguson said, adding that Moore tends to emphasize “messaging” over governing. “Comms is dictating policy, and policy is not dictating comms.” He did, however, credit Moore with working to speedily rebuild the Francis Scott Key Bridge. Its collapse, in 2024, killed six people and is the most significant catastrophe Moore has weathered as governor. The port of Baltimore was expected to be shut down for many months, but the state got it open again after less than three. Chip Somodevilla / Getty Governor Moore speaking at a commemoration ceremony at the Francis Scott Key Bridge, March, 2025. Moore is expected to win a second term in November, but the public’s mistrust has taken a political toll. The Sun and others have accused him of not being forthcoming about the state’s budget, which has seesawed from deficit to surplus to deficit again during his tenure. His vetoing of the reparations bill made some of his core supporters feel that he had misled them. When Moore’s approval rating declined, poll respondents listed the budget and the governor’s trustworthiness among their top concerns. Something about Moore does feel protean . He’s hard to place. His background can be confusing. Although he’s often compared to Obama, his education was far less rarefied. Obama was the president of the Harvard Law Review ; Moore went to junior college before landing at Johns Hopkins. He describes his upbringing as working-class—“a very hardworking family, but it was definitely a working-class family.” Perhaps by income, but by few other definitions. Both parents were college graduates. His father was an anchorman at a radio station and his mother wrote for radio and TV. Although Moore frequently says that she didn’t have a job with benefits until he was a teenager, she had won a Peabody Award and taught journalism at Howard University before he was born. Still, he saw himself as an outsider, and wouldn’t invite his friends from Riverdale back to his neighborhood. He told me that he thought very strategically about fitting in: “Okay, how do I adapt and adjust so I don’t stick out?” At Valley Forge, he was taught how to mingle with the powerful—how to walk, eat, and speak. As a high-ranking cadet, he attended lunches with former presidents, including Gerald Ford and George H. W. Bush. He said he eventually learned to accept that he was different and to be “comfortable in my own skin.” In two separate conversations, he quoted the same Jay-Z line: “I’m comfortable, dog, Brooklyn to Rome.” But he enunciated every word, in a way that sounded stiff. Despite his charisma onstage, up close, he has no swag. Where he seemed most at home was at the matcha café in Baltimore owned by an old friend of his, who surprised him with a Jamaican sorrel—a tart iced drink. “This right here would make my grandmother proud,” he said. Once, I made a Bernie Mac reference, and he got it immediately, and we shared a knowing laugh. Above all, he was comfortable talking about religion. “I come from a whole long line of preachers and teachers,” he said. “My great-grandfather was a minister; my grandfather was a minister.” In the summers, he used to stay in his grandfather’s parsonage in Brooklyn. When he told his grandmother that he was running for office, she said, “When you’re done with that, maybe you can become a minister.” “Asking me not to talk about or to acknowledge God is like asking me not to breathe air,” he told me. Don Smallwood for The Atlantic When I asked his mother, Joy Moore, if she thought he would run for president, she said: “I think his faith will take him wherever he’s going to eventually go.” She seemed more annoyed by the questions about his honesty and integrity than Moore was. “They question things that are so personal,” she said. She felt as if the articles interrogating their family history were accusing them all—her grandfather, her father, herself, her son—of being liars. And the Oxford thesis? “I mean, if he knew he was going to one day run for governor, don’t you think he would have kept stuff like that?” [ Read: Something is happening in the Democratic base ] Moore says he’d had no plans to go into politics before 2022. It was his wife, Dawn, who was the political operative, a campaign strategist who’d worked for two lieutenant governors. She and Moore eloped when he was on leave from his service in Afghanistan. While they were dating, she was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, and I was curious about whether she found divulging it to him hard. After all, I know plenty of men who wouldn’t stick around for the common cold. She said she asked him: “How would you feel if you had to take care of me for the rest of your life?” And he said: “How would you feel, if you had to take care of me for the rest of my life?” Some of the questions regarding Moore’s authenticity amount to a nebulous discomfort with how he comes across, a discomfort I recognize from all the times I’ve encountered it myself. Many people who work in elite careers after growing up relatively disadvantaged, as well as Black people who spend time in primarily white spaces, are accused of not being true to themselves. This is a false dichotomy. We can be true to ourselves while also understanding that success requires us to be supple and adaptable, and to present different aspects of our personalities at different times. There’s a famous poem by Paul Laurence Dunbar called “ We Wear the Mask ,” about the way Black Americans shield themselves from racism. I mentioned it to Moore, and he recognized it immediately. “The mask is heavy,” he said. Moore says he wears his own mask around many people, “not because it makes me more comfortable—it’s because it makes them more comfortable.” Being in spaces where people are “not used to seeing you” is a burden, he said. Being “an enigma” is a burden. “To some people, your presence is inspirational. To certain people, your presence is offensive. To certain people, your presence means progress. To certain people, your presence means we’ve lost something.” You’re a first, or you’re a threat. “That weight does sit on you,” he said. “And it’s heavy.”

items.title: Burkina: plus de 1,31 million de PDI ont regagné leur localités d’origine
items.description: (Ouagadougou, le 24 juillet 2026) L'un des principaux enseignements de l'évaluation à mi-parcours du contrat d'objectifs 2026 du Ministère de la Famille et de la Solidarité demeure la dynamique encourageante de retour des personnes déplacées internes dans leurs localités d'origine. Au 30 juin 2026, plus de 1 310 000 personnes avaient regagné 1 034 localités, contre 1 160 000 personnes dans 871 localités au 31 décembre 2025. Cette évolution traduit l'amélioration progressive de la situation dans plusieurs zones du pays ainsi que les efforts déployés par le Gouvernement pour accompagner le retour des populations. Ce contexte a conduit le Camarade Premier Ministre à donner une orientation majeure au Ministère de la Famille et de la Solidarité: Privilégier désormais la réhabilitation des habitations dans les villages de retour plutôt que la construction de logements dans les sites de déplacement, afin de consolider durablement la réinstallation des populations. Cette dynamique est accompagnée par plusieurs initiatives structurantes, notamment le renforcement des capacités du Conseil national de secours d’urgence et de réhabilitation (CONASUR) avec l’acquisition de 68 camions, la campagne nationale Dèmè Sira, le lancement de sa plateforme numérique ainsi que la phase pilote du Service social mobile. Pour le Camarade Ministre toutes ces actions traduisent la volonté du Ministère d’aller au-delà de l’assistance d’urgence pour promouvoir le relèvement, la résilience et l’autonomisation des communautés. Elle a réaffirmé son engagement à poursuivre cette dynamique aux côtés de l'ensemble des partenaires afin que chaque famille retournée retrouve progressivement des conditions de vie dignes et durables. DCRP/MFS L’article Burkina: plus de 1,31 million de PDI ont regagné leur localités d’origine est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Poni: La commune de Gaoua renforce le dialogue avec les citoyens à travers une journée de redevabilité
items.description: BURKINA-PONI-JOURNEE-REDEVABILITE Poni: La commune de Gaoua renforce le dialogue avec les citoyens à travers une journée de redevabilité Gaoua, 23 juil. 2026 (AIB) – La délégation spéciale de la commune de Gaoua a organisé, le jeudi 23 juillet 2026, une journée de dialogue et de redevabilité consacrée à la présentation du bilan de sa gestion 2025. Cette rencontre a permis aux autorités communales, aux acteurs de la société civile et aux populations d'échanger sur les réalisations enregistrées et les défis à relever pour un développement local. Selon le président de la délégation spéciale de la commune de Gaoua, Siaka Ouattara, cette initiative vise à renforcer la transparence dans la gestion communale et à consolider la confiance entre les gestionnaires de la collectivité et les citoyens. « Il faut qu'à un moment donné de la gestion de la commune, nous fassions une halte pour faire le point afin de permettre aux uns et aux autres de comprendre ce qui est fait. Cela permet de renforcer davantage la confiance entre les gestionnaires et la population », a-t-il expliqué. Pour lui, cette journée a permis de présenter les principales actions réalisées au cours de l'année 2025, notamment des investissements destinés à renforcer les capacités financières et économiques de la commune ainsi que la réalisation d'infrastructures structurantes et marchandes au profit des populations. « Toutes ces réalisations visent à impulser davantage le développement au niveau local », a-t-il indiqué, réaffirmant la volonté des autorités communales de poursuivre les efforts engagés au bénéfice des populations. Cette journée de dialogue et de redevabilité traduit la volonté de la commune de Gaoua de promouvoir une gouvernance locale participative fondée sur la transparence, le dialogue et l'implication citoyenne au service du développement durable de la collectivité. Agence d'information du Burkina MS/bak

items.title: Burkina Faso : La 1ʳᵉ édition du « Festival Boulgou » célèbre la culture bissa et la cohésion sociale à Garango
items.description: La ville de Garango, dans la région du Nakambé, a vibré du 23 au 25 juillet 2026 au rythme de la première édition du « Festival Boulgou ». Initiée par Jules Bambara, cette manifestation dédiée à la promotion de la culture bissa s'est refermée en présence des autorités administratives, coutumières, religieuses et des représentants des parrains. Le Haut-Commissaire de la province du Boulgou, Domèbèguirè Constantin Dabiré, représentant le gouverneur de la région du Nakambé, a procédé à la clôture de cette première édition du Festival Boulgou au soir du samedi 25 juillet 2026, sur le terrain de Bougoula à Garango. Durant trois jours, le « bissako » (la culture bissa) a été valorisé dans sa richesse et sa diversité à travers des danses traditionnelles, des contes, des jeux ancestraux, des prestations artisanales et le savoir-faire local. « « Festival Boulgou » est l’appellation choisie pour cette manifestation par respect aux sacrifices faits au mont Boulgou une fois par an, regroupant des milliers de personnes », a expliqué le promoteur. En rappel, le mont Boulgou est la colline sacrée qui a donné son nom à la province. Dans son allocution, le promoteur a souligné que le festival répond à la dynamique actuelle du gouvernement burkinabè visant à valoriser les savoirs endogènes. Il a ajouté qu’au-delà de son caractère festif, cet événement constitue un cadre de promotion du tourisme local, de soutien aux acteurs culturels, de valorisation des artisans, de promotion des produits locaux et de dynamisation de l’économie provinciale. Le festival a d’ailleurs servi de cadre à une exposition foraine au profit des festivaliers. Jules Bambara, Promoteur du Festival Boulgou Le camarade Birba, Directeur régional de la Construction et de la Patrie du Nakambé, représentant les parrains, le camarade Ministre des Mines et des Carrières et le camarade Directeur général de la LONAB, a quant à lui invité la jeunesse à retourner aux sources. Il a salué la pluie torrentielle tombée avant la clôture, y voyant la réponse des ancêtres aux sacrifices qui leur ont été faits. La soirée a également été marquée par des prestations d’artistes locaux mettant en valeur le style tradi-moderne et par la remise de prix aux gagnants des différentes compétitions. Le camarade Haut-Commissaire, patron de la cérémonie, a félicité le promoteur pour la réussite de l’initiative. « À travers la mise en valeur de la culture bissa, notamment par la musique et la gastronomie, vous avez su magnifier notre identité et renforcer les liens de fraternité entre les fils et filles du Boulgou » , a-t-il déclaré, avant d'ajouter : « Ce festival a démontré une fois de plus que la culture est un puissant levier de cohésion sociale, de paix et de développement local ». Les festivaliers venus de toutes parts ont exprimé leur satisfaction, à l’instar de Zaliatou Zeba, venue de Sanogo. « Je suis très contente d'être ici et j’encourage de telles initiatives, car elles rassemblent. », a-t-elle confié. Quant au jeune Olivier Lompo, venu en famille, il a confié : « Je suis très content parce qu’il y a du monde, je veux revenir ici l’an prochain ». Durant trois jours d’affilée, la ville de Garango a vécu au rythme du « bissako », l’expression de la fierté du peuple bissa. En synergie, le camarade Haut-Commissaire et le camarade Président de la Délégation spéciale ont formulé le vœu que les prochaines éditions soient encore plus ambitieuses et rayonnantes. Faso7 L’article Burkina Faso : La 1ʳᵉ édition du « Festival Boulgou » célèbre la culture bissa et la cohésion sociale à Garango est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Cameroun : l’acte 9 du SIARC s’ouvre à Yaoundé
items.description: © DR La neuvième édition du Salon international de l'Artisanat du Cameroun démarre ce 27 juillet 2026 au Musée national à Yaoundé. Cette édition met l'accent sur l'innovation comme moyen pour transformer le secteur artisanal camerounais. Importante plateforme nationale de promotion, de valorisation et de commercialisation des produits artisanaux, le SIARC démarre ce lundi à Yaoundé. Placé sous le thème «Entre tradition et modernité : comment stimuler l'innovation artisanale ?», la neuvième édition qui s'ouvre rassemble plus de 600 artisans venus du Cameroun et de plusieurs autres pays. Ils mettent leurs créations en vitrine devant des milliers de visiteurs et d'acheteurs, de professionnels, d’investisseurs, des établissements financiers, des chercheurs, des partenaires, techniques et financiers, des représentants d'institutions publiques et privées. De nombreuses délégations étrangères ont fait le déplacement pour participer au salon. L'Algérie et la Côte d'Ivoire sont les deux pays invités d'honneur à cette édition. Jusqu'au 05 août 2026, les activités tournent autour de l'exposition, mais pas seulement. Les organisateurs prévoient des conférences-débats, des ateliers de formation consacrés à l'innovation, au marketing digital, à la propriété intellectuelle, à la normalisation, à la certification et à l'accès au financement. D'autres activités comme les Journées patrimoniales mettant en exergue les dix régions du Cameroun, un espace gastronomique, des animations culturelles et le pavillon de la formalisation sont à découvrir. Les innovations annoncées au cours de cette édition sont l'ouverture d'une Boutique Souvenir du SIARC. Elle va assurer une meilleure promotion des produits labellisés du salon. Figure aussi dans ce registre des formations spécifiques sur la procédure de normalisation et de certification des produits artisanaux, des ateliers d'initiation aux métiers de l'artisanat au bénéfice des jeunes et des personnes vulnérables. D'après le ministre des PME de Économie sociale et de l'Artisanat, Achille Bassilekin III, l'artisanat demeure l'un des secteurs les plus dynamiques de l'économie camerounaise. Il mobilise près de 60% de la population active. Il participe à la création des richesses, favorise l'insertion socio-économique des milliers de Camerounais et contribue à la préservation du patrimoine culturel national. Au cours d'une conférence de presse jeudi dernier, le membre du gouvernement a indiqué que la neuvième édition du SIARC met l'accent sur la modernisation en vue de répondre aux standards internationaux. Elle donne l'occasion d'accompagner les artisans dans cette mouvance à travers plusieurs actions dont l'intégration du design contemporain, des technologies numériques, des processus de normalisation et de certification, ainsi que par le recours aux nouveaux outils de commercialisation. Ainsi, il y a lieu de préserver les traditions tout en innovant. Car l'avenir de l'artisanat camerounais repose sur sa capacité à valoriser son héritage culturel tout en s'adaptant aux mutations économiques et technologiques. Cet article Cameroun : l’acte 9 du SIARC s’ouvre à Yaoundé est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.description: Le président de l’Assemblée nationale, Dr Dansa Kourouma, a reçu, dimanche, 26 juillet, à son domicile privé de Somaya, dans la commune de Manéah (Coyah), une importante délégation des sages de la Basse-Guinée, conduite par le Kountigui, Elhadj Souna Yansané. Selon les proches du président de l’Assemblée nationale, cette délégation était venue le féliciter à la suite de son choix consensuel, le 17 juillet dernier, à la tête de l’Assemblée nationale, deuxième institution de la République. À cette occasion, les sages de la Basse-Guinée ont réitéré leur soutien à Dr Dansa Kourouma et l’ont encouragé à poursuivre ses efforts au service de la République et de l’ensemble des Guinéens. En retour, le président du Parlement a remercié la délégation et l’a invitée à prier pour le président de la République, rappelant que « lorsque le chef n’est pas à l’aise, le pays ne peut pas l’être non plus ». Il a également demandé des prières pour les députés, afin que la 10ᵉ législature accomplisse sa mission avec succès, ainsi que pour la paix et la prospérité de la Guinée. « Si nous gâtons, si nous nous trompons et que vous ne nous en parlez pas, Dieu sera notre témoin. Si vous nous trouvez sur le mauvais chemin, dites-nous : “Ça, ce n’est pas bon.” », a déclaré, en langue soussou, Dr Dansa Kourouma. Figure bien connue de la société civile guinéenne, Dr Dansa Kourouma a présidé le Conseil national de la transition (CNT) depuis sa mise en place par le CNRD, avant d’être porté à la tête de l’Assemblée nationale. items.title: AES : La Force unifiée montera en puissance de 5 000 à 18 000 soldats
items.description: La Confédération des États du Sahel (AES) s’apprête à muscler son dispositif sécuritaire. Lors d’un entretien accordé le samedi 26 juillet 2026 à la télévision nationale nigérienne, le Général d’armée Abdourahamane Tiani, président du Niger, a annoncé que les effectifs de la Force unifiée de l’AES passeront progressivement de 5 000 à 18 000 soldats. Cette montée en puissance, décidée par les ministres de la Défense du Burkina Faso, du Mali et du Niger, s’inscrit dans une stratégie de renforcement des capacités militaires de la Confédération. L’objectif est de répondre avec davantage d’efficacité à la menace terroriste qui frappe l’espace sahélien. Installé à Niamey, l’état-major opérationnel de la Force unifiée est déjà opérationnel et a mené plusieurs interventions sur le terrain. Sans entrer dans le détail de ces actions, le chef de l’État nigérien a rappelé que les impératifs de sécurité imposent une discrétion stricte sur les plans et les opérations militaires en cours. « Nous voulons atteindre 18 000 hommes car nous mesurons pleinement l’ampleur des défis auxquels nous sommes confrontés », a déclaré Abdourahamane Tiani, à l’occasion d’un bilan des deux premières années d’existence de la Confédération des États du Sahel. Ce renforcement progressif traduit la volonté de l’AES de bâtir une défense commune plus solide et d’approfondir la coopération militaire entre ses trois membres dans la lutte contre le terrorisme.
